Supplementary Material - Workplace food environments as intervention leverage points: decision analysis of safe vegetable access for low-income workers in Hanoi

Authors: Nguyen Thi Sau, Thi Thu Giang Luu, Nguyen Huu Nhuan, Nguyen Thi Tan Loc, Cory Whitney

This supplementary material provides the full probabilistic decision model, input parameter table, and diagnostic outputs supporting the main article. All code and data are available at https://github.com/sau140288/nifam_favri_companies.

1 Decision context and model structure

We apply a probabilistic decision model to assess whether large garment factories in Hanoi, Vietnam should invest in supporting on-site vegetable access for their workers. Two intervention options are evaluated against a DoNothing baseline:

  • FarmStand: The company establishes and manages an on-campus vegetable stand, sourcing directly from contracted farmers. The company bears full establishment and annual operating costs but retains control over supply chain quality, worker access, and pricing.
  • ConnectFarm: The company facilitates connections between workers and off-site farming cooperatives, enabling direct purchasing without managing a physical stand. Establishment costs are a small fraction of FarmStand costs, but the company has less control over quality and access reliability.
  • DoNothing: No intervention. Workers rely on existing off-campus food sources. This serves as the counterfactual baseline.

The model evaluates each option in terms of its net financial benefit to the company over a five-year horizon as the Net Present Value (NPV) of the intervention relative to DoNothing. A positive NPV indicates that the intervention generates more value (or avoids more cost) than taking no action. All outputs are probability distributions, reflecting full propagation of uncertainty across all input parameters.

2 Monte Carlo simulation

We parameterised the model using expert-elicited ranges representing the 5th and 95th percentiles of each uncertain input (see Section 3, Table 1). Monte Carlo simulation with 10,000 model runs was performed using the decisionSupport R package (Luedeling et al. 2021), drawing independent samples from each input distribution per run. Costs and benefits are inflated annually using the inflation_rate parameter. All future cash flows are discounted to Net Present Value using the discount_rate.

Decision outcome variables:

  • decision_farmstand: NPV of FarmStand minus NPV of DoNothing (million VND, discounted over five years)
  • decision_connectFarm: NPV of ConnectFarm minus NPV of DoNothing (million VND, discounted over five years)
source("company_model.R")

# Fixed seed ensures reproducibility across full simulation runs
set.seed(84)

source("functions/mcSimulation.R")
company_simulation_results <- mcSimulation(
  estimate = estimate_read_csv("data/company_input.csv"),
  model_function = company_model,
  numberOfModelRuns = 10000,
  functionSyntax = "plainNames"
)

3 Input parameters

Table 1 lists all model input variables with their expert-elicited uncertainty ranges. Lower and upper bounds represent the 5th and 95th percentiles of each parameter distribution. Distribution types: pos-normal = truncated normal constrained to positive values; trunc-normal [0,1] = normal truncated to the unit interval (used for probabilities and fractions); constant = fixed value.

5 Sensitivity analysis (PLS)

We use Projection to Latent Structures (PLS) regression (fitted with the orthogonal scores algorithm via pls::plsr) to identify which input variables have the strongest influence on each NPV outcome and in which direction. Variables are ranked by their Variable Importance in Projection (VIP) score; only variables with VIP > 0.9 are shown. Bar colour indicates the direction of the standardised PLS coefficient: positive (blue) values increase NPV; negative (red) values decrease NPV.

6 Expected Value of Perfect Information (EVPI)

The Expected Value of Perfect Information (EVPI) quantifies the maximum a decision-maker should rationally invest to eliminate uncertainty about a given input variable before making the decision. High EVPI identifies variables where targeted data collection would most change or reinforce the decision. EVPI is estimated using LOESS-smoothed empirical curves across the Monte Carlo sample, parallelised across all input variables for efficiency.

7 Food environment outcomes

The food environment score aggregates the effects of each intervention on workers’ access to safe, nutritious, and diverse vegetables, estimated as a productivity-equivalent monetary value (million VND/yr). The score is computed relative to DoNothing.

8 Code and data availability

All model code, input data, and analysis scripts are archived at:

https://github.com/sau140288/nifam_favri_companies

The model is implemented in R using the decisionSupport package. Monte Carlo simulation, PLS sensitivity analysis, and EVPI are all fully reproducible from the code above with set.seed(84).

Reference: Luedeling E, Goehring L, Schiffers K, Whitney C, Fernandez E (2021). decisionSupport: Quantitative Support of Decision Making under Uncertainty. R package version 1.111. https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=decisionSupport

Whitney C, Luu TTG, Kopton J, Luedeling E. A decision-analysis framework for school garden investments in Vietnam: evaluating trade-offs for nutrition, biodiversity, and economic outcomes. Humanit Soc Sci Commun. 2026;13(1):580. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-07204-0

9 Intervention Identification and Selection

9.1 Food Environment Constraints

Through food environment mapping, we identified systemic constraints affecting LMI consumers in Hanoi spanning affordability, convenience, traceability, and trust. Existing coping strategies — informal sourcing, online purchasing, self-production, social networks — remain insufficient to ensure consistent access to safe vegetables.

9.2 Workshop Process

Four focus groups drawn from the same participant pool discussed two guiding questions:

  1. Which aspects of the food environment need improvement to better support safe vegetable consumption among LMI households in inner-city Hanoi?
  2. What feasible and context-appropriate interventions can address the identified challenges?

Candidate interventions were evaluated against three criteria: (1) feasibility, (2) expected effectiveness, and (3) availability of actors capable of implementation.

9.3 Intervention Longlist and Selection

Table S1. Candidate interventions identified during the workshop, evaluated against feasibility, actor availability, and expected effectiveness.
No Intervention Selected
1 Establishing social media groups (Facebook/Zalo) for discounted purchasing
2 Adapting PGS-based internal monitoring to reduce VietGAP certification costs
3 Technical measures and state incentive programs to reduce production and retail costs
4 Communication interventions on health benefits of safe vegetables
5 Priority cards enabling LMI consumers to purchase safe vegetables at reasonable prices
6 Training and communication on best practices across the supply chain
7 Supporting producer-consumer linkages through retail and marketing integration
8 Short supply chain via direct sale point at company campus ✓
9 Land consolidation policies to address fragmented production
10 Short supply chain via local Women’s Unions organizing residential vegetable supply

9.4 Selected Intervention

Two short supply chain interventions received the highest votes. The Women’s Union option was excluded on the third criterion — consultations confirmed that existing organizational responsibilities limit capacity for additional roles. The on-campus direct sale model was selected for modelling and piloting.
